A_serious.english: Who here will beat the great Drum of Dharma?
A_serious.problem: འཇོམས་ means destroy/shatter, parallel to 'who can dry up the river of Dharma'; 'beat the drum' turns a question about who could destroy the Dharma into one about who will proclaim it, and A's note then rationalises the drying-up line.

A_serious.english: By what conditions will this way of Dharma be explained?
A_serious.problem: In context འཆད་འགྱུར་ is 'be cut off/interrupted' (followed by 'how will the lamp blaze AGAIN'); 'explained' loses the question about the Dharma's discontinuation.

pages.note: Both render the verses fully; A misreads 'joms (destroy) as 'beat' and 'chad (be cut off) as 'explained', B gets both right.

A_serious.english: They will apply themselves diligently to buying and selling, just like householders.
A_serious.problem: ཁྱིམ་པ་རྣམས་ begins a new line that continues on the next page ('they will teach/show householders'); A invents a comparison 'just like householders'.

pages.note: Both translations are close to the Tibetan; A's only real slip is the invented 'just like householders' at the page break, which B leaves correctly as a dangling 'Householders'.

A_serious.english: The kings, merchants, and Brahmins will abandon the entire kingdom. They will go to the Jewel Island and remain in a state of indifference.
A_serious.problem: The gods (ལྷ་རྣམས་) are the ones who abandon the kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, brahmins and the whole country and go to the Jewel Island; A makes the castes the subject, breaking the logic of the following 'when all the gods depart, great terror arises'.

pages.note: B correctly has the deities abandon the castes and the kingdom; A turns the castes into the ones leaving, and its added note at the top ('the path to lower realms') is speculation, not on the page.
